title: Magic ring versus starting chain
subtitle: Two ways to open a round — when each one is right
excerpt: Round work can start from a magic ring or from a chain joined in a circle. The magic ring closes to a tight centre; the chain-ring centre has a hole. Which you use depends on whether the pattern wants a closed centre or a visible opening.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886) — chain-ring foundation for medallion work. The magic ring is a twentieth-century refinement attributed to Japanese crochet pattern books.

glossaryTerms.definition: A short length of chain (usually 4-6 chains) joined with a slip stitch into a ring, which becomes the centre of a circular piece. The ring has a visible hole at the centre.
The gap at the middle of a round piece where the starting chain ring was. On a granny square the centre hole is a design feature; on an amigurumi head it needs to close completely.

heroPrompt: Two small flat crochet circles side by side on a pale surface — the left started from a chain ring with a small visible hole at the centre, the right started from a magic ring with a closed tight centre. Both in cream DK cotton.

content.text: Two standard ways to begin a crochet circle. The

— chain 4 or 6, join with a slip stitch — has been in crochet pattern books since the nineteenth century. The magic ring is newer: an adjustable loop that tightens to a closed centre. Both work; they give different results at the

Chain 4 (or as many as the pattern specifies). Insert the hook into the first chain made, yarn over, pull through — this joins the chain into a circle. Work the stitches of round 1 into the centre of the ring (not into individual chains). At the end of the round, join with a slip stitch as normal.

The chain ring leaves a small hole at the centre of the piece. On granny squares and flat motifs this is a design feature — the hole is part of the traditional pattern. On hats the hole is at the top of the crown, which some patterns patch with a sewn close; others just leave it. A 4-chain ring gives a smaller hole than a 6-chain ring.

The magic ring is an adjustable loop: make a loop around two fingers, insert the hook through the loop, and work the stitches of round 1 over the loop strand. After round 1 is complete, pull the yarn tail to close the loop tight before joining. The centre closes to almost nothing — the right choice for amigurumi heads, animal ears, and any piece where a hole at the centre is a defect rather than a feature.
Granny squares, traditional motifs, vintage patterns: chain ring. The hole is part of the design.
Amigurumi, stuffed pieces, hats where a closed crown is wanted: magic ring.
Pattern says 'ch 4, join with sl st to form a ring': use chain ring exactly as written.
Pattern says 'magic ring' or 'adjustable ring': use magic ring. The two are not interchangeable for tight-centre work.

attrs.title: Struggling with the magic ring?
attrs.body: Start with a chain ring on your first few round projects. The magic ring is a fine motor skill that takes a few tries to feel natural. Once you can see clearly how the centre of a chain-ring piece looks versus a magic-ring piece, the reason to learn the magic ring becomes obvious.
